To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the costs of dying are a consequence of moral-hazard-induced over-consumption of health-care services and that a coinsurance scheme can be designed to prevent age-related moral hazard.

the optimal insurance policy is a coinsurance scheme that links the coinsurance to the age-specific probability of dying and that the optimal coinsurance rate is increasing with the age-specific mortality probability.

(i) high costs of dying are caused by moral hazard, (ii) moral hazard can be reduced by a coinsurance system that links the coinsurance ratio to the age-specific residual life expectancy, and (iii) a coinsurance system with age-dependent coinsurance rates can be implemented by means of a health-care system that links the insurance premium to the age-specific risk of dying
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the costs of dying are an argument for rationing.
the moral hazard problem that arises in the last stage of life, when the insured is confronted with high medical bills and low residual life expectancy.
the question of how the costs of dying can be reduced without rationing health-care services.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the costs of dying are a consequence of moral hazards and can be limited by coinsurance schemes that are adapted to individual age-specific mortality risks.
the costs of dying are not a reason for rationing health-care services according the age of the patients.
the high costs of health care for dying individuals can be reduced by a coinsurance policy that increases the coinsurance rate with the age of an insured person.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high costs of dying can be avoided by an insurance policy that takes account of the individual's age-specific mortality risk, and by a coinsurance rate that is age-related.
a high coinsurance rate for the elderly can reduce the high costs of health care at the end of life and thus reduce the moral hazard problem in health care.
the high costs of health care for the dying are due to moral hazard and can be avoided by an age-dependent coinsurance scheme.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the costs of dying can be reduced by means of a coinsurance scheme that is based on the insured's age and mortality risk.
the costs of dying do not justify a rationing of medical services for the elderly.
a coinsurance scheme that increases with the insured's age is a more efficient alternative to rationing health care according to age.
